questions.question: Which layer does HTTP belong to?
options: Data format
Style / protocol
Transport
Authentication
questions.explanation: HTTP (and HTTPS) is the transport layer — how bytes actually travel between client and server. REST/SOAP are the style layer, and JSON/XML are the data format layer.

questions.question: Which statement best describes REST?
options: A strict XML-only protocol with a formal WSDL contract
An architectural style where each resource has a URL and HTTP methods act on it, usually with JSON
A data format for encoding binary files
A Salesforce-specific authentication mechanism
questions.explanation: REST is a style, not a strict standard — resources have URLs, HTTP methods act on them, and it's usually (not exclusively) JSON over HTTP(S).

questions.question: Which statement best describes SOAP?
options: A lightweight style with no formal contract
A stricter protocol using XML envelopes and a WSDL-described contract
A transport layer alternative to HTTP
A JSON-based messaging format
questions.explanation: SOAP is a stricter protocol: XML envelopes, a formal WSDL contract, and built-in standards like WS-Security.

questions.question: In Apex, what happens when a callout receives a 404 response?
options: Apex automatically throws a CalloutException
The transaction is automatically rolled back
Nothing automatic — getStatusCode() returns 404, and your code must check it
The response body is automatically discarded
questions.explanation: A 404 (or any status code) doesn't throw by itself in Apex — it's just a number returned by getStatusCode(). Checking it is the caller's responsibility.

questions.question: Why is 'use SOAP because it feels more enterprise' usually bad advice for a new integration?
options: SOAP cannot be used with Salesforce at all
SOAP always travels over a different transport than HTTP
Unless there's an explicit requirement to match a SOAP/WSDL contract, REST is simpler, lighter, and better supported by modern tooling
SOAP doesn't support authentication
questions.explanation: The rule of thumb is to default to REST for new work, and only reach for SOAP when the other system requires it — not for its own sake.
